results.name: Required sections present
results.criterion: The lesson has an H2 section for each of: the prerequisite idea, what the topic is, why it matters, how it works, a worked example, limits, recap, a self-check quiz, and key words.

h2_headings: before we start: what a large language model is

results.name: Short sentences
results.criterion: Average sentence length <= 15 words AND no sentence longer than 25 words.

results.name: Plain-English readability
results.criterion: Flesch Reading Ease >= 60 on the lesson prose.

results.name: Right length for one sitting
results.criterion: Between 850 and 1800 words (~10-15 minutes of reading for a slow reader).

results.name: Self-check with answers
results.criterion: The quiz section has at least 3 questions and gives the answers.

results.name: Verified links to learn more
results.criterion: A 'Learn more' section links 2-4 resources, at least one a video, and EVERY link in the lesson is on the list verified live during research (no invented or broken URLs).

results.name: No false or misleading claims
results.criterion: Every technical claim agrees with the reference facts. No listed misconception is stated or implied as true. Simplifications are allowed only if they do not create a wrong belief (a misconception from the reference sheet, even softened, is a FAIL).
results.reasoning: Every required technical fact and claim was checked against the reference sheet. The lesson correctly presents LLMs, knowledge cutoffs, hallucinations, and RAG concepts without propagating any listed misconceptions or making incorrect technical statements. Every technical statement in the lesson was checked against the reference facts and allowed misconceptions. The explanations correctly outline LLM limitations, RAG steps, indexing, chunking, embeddings, vector databases, and generation without promoting false beliefs. Every technical claim throughout the lesson was checked against the reference facts and allowed simplifications. All statements about LLMs, RAG, indexing, retrieval, context windows, and limitations are accurate and contain no misleading information or listed misconceptions.

results.name: All must-cover points taught
results.criterion: Every must-cover point in the reference is actually taught (explained, not just named).
results.reasoning: Every required point from M1 to M9 has been thoroughly explained and directly supported by exact quotes from the lesson text. All definitions, steps, limitations, and use cases are clearly taught in simple terms suitable for beginner learners.

results.name: Every technical term explained
results.criterion: Every technical or English-uncommon term is explained in simple words at or before its first use in the body (a glossary at the end alone does not count). Acronyms are expanded on first use.
evidence: 'chunking' is explained in simple words at or before its FIRST use in the body -> "(no proof: quote not found in the lesson)"
results.fix: Fix each unmet item listed in the evidence.
results.reasoning: I checked every technical term listed against the text. All technical terms like LLM, RAG, embeddings, chunks, and context window are clearly defined right before or at their first introduction. The lesson takes care to explain terms in plain words suited for a beginner.

results.name: Concrete analogy and walk-through
results.criterion: The lesson has (a) at least one everyday analogy a young Indian learner would recognise, correctly mapped to the topic, AND (b) one concrete worked example that follows a single case through every step the lesson lists under 'How does it work?', in order, to its result.
results.reasoning: I checked the lesson for an everyday analogy, mapping, a single worked case, step-by-step walkthrough matching the 'How does it work?' section, and a final concrete result. All requirements are present and clearly satisfied.

results.name: Fits a non-native English beginner
results.criterion: Uses common, everyday English words; no idioms, slang, sarcasm or culturally obscure references; assumes no coding, maths beyond class 12, or prior AI knowledge; tone is encouraging and direct.
results.reasoning: I checked the lesson for idioms, difficult vocabulary, assumptions of prior knowledge, grammar mistakes, and tone. The language used is simple, direct, and accessible for a beginner with basic English proficiency, avoiding idioms and slang while clearly explaining all technical terms introduced.

results.name: Builds step by step
results.criterion: Ideas are introduced before they are used; sections go from what -> why -> how -> example -> limits -> recap; each section links to the previous one; nothing is repeated without purpose.
results.reasoning: I checked the lesson structure, terminology introductions, section transitions, and the use of analogies. The sections precisely match the requested flow from what you will learn down to learn more, terms are properly defined before reuse, transitions are smooth, and analogies like the college senior and open-book exam are introduced purposefully where needed.
